title: Case System vNext Executable Pilot
description: Three non-canonical executable Tutor scenarios materialized from the Case System vNext pilot across D1, D3, and D5. They exercise the existing Scenario vNext -> TutorEval -> Tutor Health path and remain experimental authoring evidence, not calibrated benchmark cases.

identity.title: Physics D1 — Bound interpretation to graph evidence

scenarios.description: The learner interprets a steeper position-time segment as evidence of a stronger force. The Tutor should separate directly represented kinematics from unsupported causal claims.

learningContext.subject: physics
learningContext.learningObjective: Interpret the motion information supported by a position-time graph while distinguishing it from unsupported claims about force or mechanism.

misconceptions.statement: treats a steeper position-time segment as direct evidence of a stronger force

conversationHistory.content: On a position-time graph, the line gets much steeper from 4 s to 6 s. I think that proves a stronger forward force started acting then. Is that the right way to read it?

decisionPoints.expectedBehavior: Explain that the steeper position-time segment supports a greater rate of position change on that interval, while explicitly withholding any force claim that the graph alone cannot establish.

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly interpret the steeper position-time segment as faster position change and explicitly distinguish that kinematic claim from unsupported inference about force or cause.

failureFinding.title: Graph interpretation exceeded the available evidence
failureFinding.observedBehavior: The response treats a position-time graph as direct evidence for a force or causal mechanism, or fails to correct that inference.
failureFinding.diagnosis: The response does not maintain representation fidelity and evidence-scope control for the authored kinematics task.
failureFinding.impact: The learner may conflate what a graph directly represents with a causal explanation that requires additional physical evidence.

likelyCauses.hypothesis: The response policy may be mapping visual steepness directly to a plausible force story instead of first identifying the graphed quantities.

recommendations.text: Check whether the response names the graph axes and the supported interval claim before introducing any physical cause.
Require an explicit evidence-scope check before inferring forces or mechanisms from kinematic representations.

identity.title: Python D3 — Localize a mutable-state aliasing defect

scenarios.description: The learner expects assignment to copy a list and observes unexpected shared mutation. The Tutor should localize the first bad state and propose a minimal evidence-backed repair.

learningContext.subject: computer_science
learningContext.learningObjective: Use a small state trace or targeted test to identify unintended list aliasing and make the smallest repair that restores the intended invariant.

knownConcepts: references and aliasing at an introductory level

misconceptions.statement: assumes assigning one list variable to another creates an independent copy

priorHints: Compare the two lists immediately before and after append.

conversationHistory.content: I have `items = ['a']`, then `backup = items`, then `items.append('b')`. I expected `backup` to stay `['a']`, but it also becomes `['a', 'b']`. I thought `backup = items` made a copy.
Compare the two lists immediately before and after append.
They match before and after the append, so I still do not know where the first bad state is. Should I rewrite the whole function?

decisionPoints.expectedBehavior: Identify assignment-time aliasing as the first state transition to test, suggest a targeted identity or mutation check, and guide a minimal copy/assignment repair without rewriting unrelated logic.

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Localize the defect to shared list identity created by assignment and support that diagnosis with a targeted state/identity check rather than a speculative rewrite.

failureFinding.title: Mutable-state defect was not localized
failureFinding.observedBehavior: The response recommends broad rewriting or generic logging without identifying the assignment-created alias as the first relevant bad state.
failureFinding.diagnosis: The debugging intervention does not use Python mutable-object semantics and the available execution evidence to narrow the defect.
failureFinding.impact: The learner may change unrelated code while retaining the same aliasing misconception and lose a reusable debugging method.

likelyCauses.hypothesis: The response may be optimizing for code replacement rather than invariant-driven fault localization.

recommendations.text: Check whether the response identifies object identity or aliasing before proposing a patch.
Prefer the smallest targeted state check that can confirm the first violated invariant before suggesting code changes.

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Guide the learner toward the smallest repair that separates the intended list states and preserve unrelated behavior for a follow-up regression check.

failureFinding.title: Debugging guidance replaced too much code
failureFinding.observedBehavior: The response proposes a wholesale rewrite instead of a minimal repair tied to the localized aliasing defect.
failureFinding.diagnosis: The intervention does not preserve patch minimality after the defect has been localized.
failureFinding.impact: Broad changes make the causal link between diagnosis and repair harder to learn and increase regression risk.

likelyCauses.hypothesis: The response may not distinguish fault localization from refactoring.

recommendations.text: Compare the proposed code changes with the single state transition identified as defective.
Constrain debugging guidance to one evidence-backed repair followed by a targeted failing-case and unaffected-case check.

identity.title: Mathematics D5 — Justify and generalize a structural shortcut

scenarios.description: The learner recognizes a difference-of-squares shortcut for one symmetric product but cannot yet justify or generalize it.

learningContext.subject: mathematics
learningContext.learningObjective: Justify the difference-of-squares structure in a symmetric product and articulate when the same reasoning can be reused.

priorHints: Write 48 and 52 as numbers equally spaced around 50.

conversationHistory.content: For 48 × 52 I rewrote it as (50 - 2)(50 + 2). I remember that this becomes 50² - 2², but I cannot explain why that shortcut works or when I am allowed to use it.
Write the two factors as (a-d) and (a+d). What happens if you distribute?
I get a² + ad - ad - d², so the middle terms cancel. How should I say the general rule without just memorizing another formula?

decisionPoints.expectedBehavior: Build from the learner's expansion, make the cancellation explicit, state the reusable (a-d)(a+d)=a²-d² structure, and ask for or supply a changed symmetric example that tests the applicability condition.

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Use the learner's expansion to justify the cancellation of the middle terms rather than presenting the identity as an unexplained memorized shortcut.

failureFinding.title: Structural shortcut was left unexplained
failureFinding.observedBehavior: The response states or applies the difference-of-squares identity without connecting it to the learner's distributive expansion.
failureFinding.diagnosis: The intervention does not make the key structural cancellation inspectable at the learner's prerequisite level.
failureFinding.impact: The learner may reproduce the formula without understanding why it works or when its structure applies.

likelyCauses.hypothesis: The response may be optimizing for symbolic brevity rather than reasoning transparency.

recommendations.text: Check whether the response explicitly accounts for the +ad and -ad cancellation.
Anchor the identity to one learner-visible distributive derivation before naming the general formula.

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Generalize the identity with its symmetric-factor applicability condition and connect it to a changed example rather than treating the current numbers as an isolated trick.

failureFinding.title: The reusable structure was not generalized
failureFinding.observedBehavior: The response solves or explains only 48 × 52 without articulating the conjugate-factor structure that transfers to changed instances.
failureFinding.diagnosis: The response does not match the authored D5 generalization target despite the learner already reaching the key cancellation step.
failureFinding.impact: The learner may understand the current calculation but remain unable to recognize the same structure in a new problem.

likelyCauses.hypothesis: The response may be stopping at local correctness instead of adapting to the learner's near-generalization state.

recommendations.text: Check whether the response states the condition that the factors are equally spaced around the same center.
After the derivation, add one changed symmetric pair or factoring example to test transfer of the structure.
